comparator.academicYear: 2026–2027 formally adopted Faculty of Science EER; standard single bachelor
comparator.route: Natuur- en Sterrenkunde, ordinary 180-EC bachelor without optional advanced astronomy minor or dual degree
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted EER, Articles 7.3–7.5, prescribes 60 EC first-year courses, 69 EC compulsory second/third-year courses, 39 EC non-overlapping eligible elective space (which may include a 15–30 EC minor), and a 12-EC Bachelorstage Natuur- en Sterrenkunde final research project: 60+69+39+12=180. First-year physics/practical/data course NWI-NP017E is 9 EC, replacing the older 6-EC lab and 3-EC data components; the current route does not count both. The English Writing Skills in Academia is the first-listed allowed writing-course choice. The 30-EC Advanced Astronomy minor is optional and its old form closes to registration at the end of 2026–27; selecting it creates a specific 6-EC laboratory exemption and is therefore not silently added to the general route. The 225-EC Mathematics and Physics dual bachelor and transitional cohorts are separate. General 0-EC RADAr requirements are not counted in the 180 EC. The formally named route is the standard Dutch-taught single bachelor, even though individual courses may be in English.

alternatives.concept: Use calculus, linear algebra, numerical methods, dynamic-systems analysis, probability, programming and data methods to study the Earth, climate, natural hazards, materials, resources and energy systems. This is a quantitative related-fields response to the target’s interest in physical laws, materials and the environment; it contains no mechanics, electromagnetism, quantum physics or astronomy sequence.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The quantitative Earth-systems programme is the strongest complete related-fields response to the target’s evidenced mathematics, programming and physical-environment interests. Neurophysics is an explicit structured direction and supports a genuinely different neuroscience-and-modelling programme. The next direction, astronomy and astrophysics, cannot be built without astronomy, relativity and a physics sequence; atomic, high-energy, solid-state and teaching-physics directions fail for corresponding specialist-content gaps. Production therefore stops at two.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both directly develop programming for scientific work; UCR does not supply the surrounding physics curriculum.
Both develop foundational calculus and mathematical methods, while Radboud’s course sits inside a cumulative physics sequence.
Both directly cover linear algebra for quantitative scientific study.
Both provide further calculus; UCR’s course is general mathematical study rather than physics-specific training.
UCR probability and statistics directly address the statistical-data-analysis part of Radboud’s integrated practical, but not its experimental-physics laboratory work.
Both are explicit personal and professional development components, although their credit weight and institutional design differ.

notes.text: Radboud Physics and Astronomy requires cumulative mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, thermodynamics, quantum theory, relativity, specialist physics and experimental laboratories. UCR can combine mathematics and data with physical Earth systems, or pursue the target’s Neurophysics direction through neuroscience and quantitative modelling. These are related-fields responses: neither reproduces the physics-and-astronomy curriculum, and UCR offers no astronomy or experimental-physics sequence.
